title: If I should have a daughter ...
speaker: Sarah Kay

sentences.en: If I should have a daughter, instead of "Mom," she's going to call me "Point B," because that way she knows that no matter what happens, at least she can always find her way to me.
And I'm going to paint solar systems on the backs of her hands so she has to learn the entire universe before she can say, "Oh, I know that like the back of my hand."
And she's going to learn that this life will hit you hard in the face, wait for you to get back up just so it can kick you in the stomach.
But getting the wind knocked out of you is the only way to remind your lungs how much they like the taste of air.
There is hurt, here, that cannot be fixed by Band-Aids or poetry.

So the first time she realizes that Wonder Woman isn't coming, I'll make sure she knows she doesn't have to wear the cape all by herself, because no matter how wide you stretch your fingers, your hands will always be too small
to catch all the pain you want to heal. Believe me, I've tried.
"And, baby," I'll tell her, don't keep your nose up in the air like that.
I know that trick; I've done it a million times.
You're just smelling for smoke so you can follow the trail back to a burning house, so you can find the boy who lost everything in the fire to see if you can save him.
Or else find the boy who lit the fire in the first place, to see if you can change him.
But I know she will anyway, so instead I'll always keep an extra supply of chocolate and rain boots nearby, because there is no heartbreak that chocolate can't fix.
Okay, there's a few that chocolate can't fix.
But that's what the rain boots are for, because rain will wash away everything, if you let it.

I want her to look at the world through the underside of a glass-bottom boat, to look through a microscope at the galaxies that exist on the pinpoint of a human mind, because that's the way my mom taught me.
That there'll be days like this. (Singing) There'll be days like this, my momma said.

When you open your hands to catch and wind up with only blisters and bruises; when you step out of the phone booth and try to fly and the very people you want to save are the ones standing on your cape; when your boots will fill with rain,
and you'll be up to your knees in disappointment.
And those are the very days you have all the more reason to say thank you.
Because there's nothing more beautiful than the way the ocean refuses to stop kissing the shoreline, no matter how many times it's sent away.
You will put the wind in win some, lose some.
You will put the star in starting over, and over.
And no matter how many land mines erupt in a minute, be sure your mind lands on the beauty of this funny place called life.
And yes, on a scale from one to over-trusting, I am pretty damn naive.
But I want her to know that this world is made out of sugar.
It can crumble so easily, but don't be afraid to stick your tongue out and taste it.
"Baby," I'll tell her, "remember, your momma is a worrier, and your poppa is a warrior, and you are the girl with small hands and big eyes who never stops asking for more."
Remember that good things come in threes and so do bad things.
Always apologize when you've done something wrong, but don't you ever apologize for the way your eyes refuse to stop shining.
Your voice is small, but don't ever stop singing.

And when they finally hand you heartache, when they slip war and hatred under your door and offer you handouts on street-corners of cynicism and defeat, you tell them that they really ought to meet your mother.
(Applause) Thank you. Thank you. (Applause) Thank you.
(Applause) Thanks. (Applause) Thank you.
(Applause) All right, so I want you to take a moment, and I want you to think of three things that you know to be true.
They can be about whatever you want -- technology, entertainment, design, your family, what you had for breakfast.
The only rule is don't think too hard. Okay, ready? Go.
Okay. So here are three things I know to be true.
I know that Jean-Luc Godard was right when he said that, "A good story has a beginning, a middle and an end, although not necessarily in that order."
I know that I'm incredibly nervous and excited to be up here, which is greatly inhibiting my ability to keep it cool.
(Laughter) And I know that I have been waiting all week to tell this joke.
(Laughter) Why was the scarecrow invited to TED?
Because he was out standing in his field.
(Laughter) I'm sorry. Okay, so these are three things I know to be true.
But there are plenty of things I have trouble understanding.
So I write poems to figure things out. Sometimes the only way I know how to work through something is by writing a poem.

Sometimes I get to the end of the poem, look back and go, "Oh, that's what this is all about," and sometimes I get to the end of the poem and haven't solved anything, but at least I have a new poem out of it.
Spoken-word poetry is the art of performance poetry.
I tell people it involves creating poetry that doesn't just want to sit on paper, that something about it demands it be heard out loud or witnessed in person.
When I was a freshman in high school, I was a live wire of nervous hormones.
And I was underdeveloped and over-excitable.
And despite my fear of ever being looked at for too long, I was fascinated by the idea of spoken-word poetry.
sentences.zh: 尽管我害怕被人注视太久，但我还是对口语诗歌的想法着迷。

sentences.en: I felt that my two secret loves, poetry and theater, had come together, had a baby, a baby I needed to get to know.
sentences.zh: 我觉得我的两个秘密爱好，诗歌和戏剧，已经走到了一起，生下了一个孩子，一个我需要了解的孩子。

sentences.en: So I decided to give it a try. My first spoken-word poem, packed with all the wisdom of a 14-year-old, was about the injustice of being seen as unfeminine.
sentences.zh: 所以我决定尝试一下。我的第一首口语诗充满了 14 岁孩子的所有智慧，是关于被视为不女性化的不公正。

sentences.en: The poem was very indignant, and mainly exaggerated, but the only spoken-word poetry that I had seen up until that point was mainly indignant, so I thought that's what was expected of me.
sentences.zh: 这首诗非常愤怒，而且主要是夸张的，但迄今为止我所见过的唯一的口头诗歌主要是愤怒的，所以我认为这就是对我的期望。

sentences.en: The first time that I performed, the audience of teenagers hooted and hollered their sympathy, and when I came off the stage, I was shaking.
sentences.zh: 我第一次表演时，台下的青少年们发出了欢呼声和同情声，当我走下舞台时，我浑身发抖。

sentences.en: I felt this tap on my shoulder, and I turned around to see this giant girl in a hoodie sweatshirt emerge from the crowd.
sentences.zh: 我感觉到有人拍了拍我的肩膀，我转身看到这个穿着连帽运动衫的巨大女孩从人群中出现。

sentences.en: She was maybe eight feet tall and looked like she could beat me up with one hand, but instead she just nodded at me and said, "Hey, I really felt that. Thanks."
sentences.zh: 她大概有八英尺高，看起来一只手就能打我，但她只是对我点点头说：“嘿，我真的有这种感觉。谢谢。”

sentences.en: And lightning struck. I was hooked. I discovered this bar on Manhattan's Lower East Side that hosted a weekly poetry open Mic, and my bewildered, but supportive, parents took me to soak in every ounce of spoken word that I could.
sentences.zh: 闪电击中了。我被迷住了。我发现了曼哈顿下东区的这家酒吧，每周举办一次诗歌开放麦克风活动，我的父母虽然困惑，但很支持我，带我尽我所能地吸收每一盎司的口语单词。

sentences.en: I was the youngest by at least a decade, but somehow the poets at the Bowery Poetry Club didn't seem bothered by the 14-year-old wandering about.
sentences.zh: 我是最年轻的，至少比我小十岁，但不知何故，包厘街诗歌俱乐部的诗人似乎并不关心这个 14 岁的流浪者。

sentences.en: In fact, they welcomed me. And it was here, listening to these poets share their stories, that I learned that spoken-word poetry didn't have to be indignant, it could be fun or painful or serious or silly.
sentences.zh: 事实上，他们很欢迎我。正是在这里，听这些诗人分享他们的故事，我才知道口语诗不一定是愤怒的，它可以是有趣的、痛苦的、严肃的或愚蠢的。

sentences.en: The Bowery Poetry Club became my classroom and my home, and the poets who performed encouraged me to share my stories as well.
sentences.zh: 包厘街诗歌俱乐部成了我的教室和我的家，表演的诗人也鼓励我分享我的故事。

sentences.en: Never mind the fact that I was 14. They told me, "Write about being 14."
sentences.zh: 别介意我已经 14 岁了。他们告诉我，“写下 14 岁的经历。”

sentences.en: So I did and stood amazed every week when these brilliant, grown-up poets laughed with me and groaned their sympathy and clapped and told me, "Hey, I really felt that too."
sentences.zh: 所以我就这样做了，每周当这些才华横溢的成年诗人与我一起大笑、呻吟着表示同情、鼓掌告诉我：“嘿，我也确实有这种感觉。”我都会感到惊讶。

sentences.en: Now I can divide my spoken-word journey into three steps.
sentences.zh: 现在我可以把我的口语之旅分为三个步骤。

sentences.en: Step one was the moment I said, "I can. I can do this."
sentences.zh: 第一步是我说：“我可以。我可以做到这一点。”

sentences.en: And that was thanks to a girl in a hoodie.
sentences.zh: 这要归功于一个穿着连帽衫的女孩。

sentences.en: Step two was the moment I said, "I will. I will continue.
sentences.zh: 第二步是我说：“我会的。我会继续。”

sentences.en: I love spoken word. I will keep coming back week after week."
sentences.zh: 我喜欢口语。我会一周又一周地回来。”

sentences.en: And step three began when I realized I didn't have to write indignant poems, if that's not what I was.
sentences.zh: 当我意识到我不必写愤怒的诗时，第三步开始了，如果那不是我的话。

sentences.en: There were things that were specific to me, and the more that I focused on those things, the weirder my poetry got, but the more that it felt like mine.
sentences.zh: 有些事情是我特有的，我越关注这些事情，我的诗就越奇怪，但它感觉起来就越像我的。

sentences.en: It's not just the adage "Write what you know."
sentences.zh: 这不仅仅是一句格言“写下你所知道的”。

sentences.en: It's about gathering up all of the knowledge and experience you've collected up to now to help you dive into the things you don't know.
sentences.zh: 它是关于收集您迄今为止收集的所有知识和经验，以帮助您深入研究您不知道的事情。

sentences.en: I use poetry to help me work through what I don't understand, but I show up to each new poem with a backpack full of everywhere else that I've been.
sentences.zh: 我用诗歌来帮助我解决我不理解的问题，但我在面对每首新诗时都会带着一个装满了我去过的其他地方的背包。

sentences.en: When I got to university, I met a fellow poet who shared my belief in the magic of spoken-word poetry.
sentences.zh: 当我上大学时，我遇到了一位诗人同伴，他和我一样相信口语诗歌的魔力。

sentences.en: And actually, Phil Kaye and I coincidentally also share the same last name.
sentences.zh: 事实上，菲尔·凯和我巧合的是也有相同的姓氏。

sentences.en: When I was in high school I had created Project V.O.I.C.E.
as a way to encourage my friends to do spoken word with me.
But Phil and I decided to reinvent Project V.O.I.C.E., this time changing the mission to using spoken-word poetry as a way to entertain, educate and inspire.

We stayed full-time students, but in between we traveled, performing and teaching nine-year-olds to MFA candidates, from California to Indiana to India to a public high school just up the street from campus.
And we saw over and over the way that spoken-word poetry cracks open locks.
But it turns out sometimes, poetry can be really scary.
Turns out sometimes, you have to trick teenagers into writing poetry.
So I came up with lists. Everyone can write lists.
And the first list that I assign is "10 Things I Know to be True."
And here's what happens, you would discover it too if we all started sharing our lists out loud.
At a certain point, you would realize that someone has the exact same thing, or one thing very similar, to something on your list.
And then someone else has something the complete opposite of yours.
Third, someone has something you've never even heard of before.
Fourth, someone has something you thought you knew everything about, but they're introducing a new angle of looking at it.
And I tell people that this is where great stories start from -- these four intersections of what you're passionate about and what others might be invested in.
And most people respond really well to this exercise.
But one of my students, a freshman named Charlotte, was not convinced.
Charlotte was very good at writing lists, but she refused to write any poems.
"Miss," she'd say, "I'm just not interesting.
I don't have anything interesting to say."
So I assigned her list after list, and one day I assigned the list "10 Things I Should Have Learned by Now."
Number three on Charlotte's list was, "I should have learned not to crush on guys three times my age."
I asked her what that meant, and she said, "Miss, it's kind of a long story."
And I said, "Charlotte, it sounds pretty interesting to me."
And so she wrote her first poem, a love poem unlike any I had ever heard before.
And the poem began, "Anderson Cooper is a gorgeous man."
(Laughter) "Did you see him on 60 Minutes, racing Michael Phelps in a pool -- nothing but swim trunks on -- diving in the water, determined to beat this swimming champion?
After the race, he tossed his wet, cloud-white hair and said, 'You're a god.'
No, Anderson, you're the god." (Laughter) (Applause) Now, I know that the number one rule to being cool is to seem unfazed,
to never admit that anything scares you or impresses you or excites you.
Somebody once told me it's like walking through life like this.
You protect yourself from all the unexpected miseries or hurt that might show up.
But I try to walk through life like this.
And yes, that means catching all of those miseries and hurt, but it also means that when beautiful, amazing things just fall out of the sky, I'm ready to catch them.

I use spoken word to help my students rediscover wonder, to fight their instincts to be cool and unfazed and, instead, actively pursue being engaged with what goes on around them, so that they can reinterpret and create something from it.
It's not that I think that spoken-word poetry is the ideal art form.
I'm always trying to find the best way to tell each story.
I write musicals; I make short films alongside my poems.
But I teach spoken-word poetry because it's accessible.
Not everyone can read music or owns a camera, but everyone can communicate in some way, and everyone has stories that the rest of us can learn from.
Plus, spoken-word poetry allows for immediate connection.

It's not uncommon to feel like you're alone or that nobody understands you, but spoken word teaches that if you have the ability to express yourself and the courage to present those stories and opinions, you could be rewarded
with a room full of your peers, or your community, who will listen.
And maybe even a giant girl in a hoodie who will connect with what you've shared.
And that is an amazing realization to have, especially when you're 14.
Plus, now with YouTube, that connection's not even limited to the room we're in.
I'm so lucky that there's this archive of performances that I can share with my students.
It allows for even more opportunities for them to find a poet or a poem that they connect to.
Once you've figured this out, it is tempting to keep writing the same poem, or keep telling the same story, over and over, once you've figured out that it will gain you applause.
It's not enough to just teach that you can express yourself.
You have to grow and explore and take risks and challenge yourself.
sentences.zh: 你必须成长、探索、冒险、挑战自己。

sentences.en: And that is step three: infusing the work you're doing with the specific things that make you you, even while those things are always changing.
sentences.zh: 这就是第三步：将你正在做的工作与那些让你成为你的具体事物相结合，即使这些事物总是在变化。

sentences.en: Because step three never ends. But you don't get to start on step three, until you take step one first: "I can."
sentences.zh: 因为第三步永远不会结束。但你不能开始第三步，除非你先迈出第一步：“我可以。”

sentences.en: I travel a lot while I'm teaching, and I don't always get to watch all of my students reach their step three, but I was very lucky with Charlotte, that I got to watch her journey unfold the way it did.
sentences.zh: 我在教学期间经常出差，我并不总是能看到我所有的学生都达到第三步，但我对夏洛特很幸运，我能看到她的旅程以它的方式展开。

sentences.en: I watched her realize that, by putting the things that she knows to be true into the work she's doing, she can create poems that only Charlotte can write, about eyeballs and elevators and Dora the Explorer.
sentences.zh: 我看着她意识到，通过将她所知道的真实事物融入到她正在做的工作中，她可以创作出只有夏洛特才能写的诗，关于眼球、电梯和探险家朵拉的诗。

sentences.en: And I'm trying to tell stories only I can tell -- like this story.
sentences.zh: 我试图讲述只有我能讲的故事——就像这个故事。

sentences.en: I spent a lot of time thinking about the best way to tell this story, and I wondered if the best way was going to be a PowerPoint, a short film -- And where exactly was the beginning, the middle or the end?
sentences.zh: 我花了很多时间思考讲述这个故事的最佳方式，我想知道最好的方式是否是一个 PowerPoint、一部短片——开头、中间或结尾到底在哪里？

sentences.en: I wondered whether I'd get to the end of this talk and finally have figured it all out, or not.
sentences.zh: 我想知道我是否能读完这次演讲并最终弄清楚一切。

sentences.en: And I always thought that my beginning was at the Bowery Poetry Club, but it's possible that it was much earlier.
sentences.zh: 我一直以为我的起点是在包厘街诗歌俱乐部，但也有可能更早。

sentences.en: In preparing for TED, I discovered this diary page in an old journal.
sentences.zh: 在准备 TED 的过程中，我在一本旧日记中发现了这篇日记。

sentences.en: I think December 54th was probably supposed to be 24th.
sentences.zh: 我认为 12 月 54 日可能应该是 24 日。

sentences.en: It's clear that when I was a child, I definitely walked through life like this.
sentences.zh: 很显然，我小时候肯定是这样走过人生的。

sentences.en: I think that we all did. I would like to help others rediscover that wonder -- to want to engage with it, to want to learn, to want to share what they've learned, what they've figured out to be true and what they're still figuring out.
sentences.zh: 我想我们都做到了。我想帮助其他人重新发现这种奇迹——想要参与其中，想要学习，想要分享他们所学到的东西，他们已经发现的真实的东西以及他们仍在弄清楚的东西。

sentences.en: So I'd like to close with this poem. When they bombed Hiroshima, the explosion formed a mini-supernova, so every living animal, human or plant
sentences.zh: 所以我想以这首诗作为结束语。当他们轰炸广岛时，爆炸形成了一颗迷你超新星，所以每一个活着的动物、人类或植物

sentences.en: that received direct contact with the rays from that sun was instantly turned to ash.
sentences.zh: 直接接触到那太阳的光芒，瞬间化为灰烬。

sentences.en: And what was left of the city soon followed.
sentences.zh: 很快，这座城市剩下的部分也随之而来。

sentences.en: The long-lasting damage of nuclear radiation caused an entire city and its population to turn into powder.
sentences.zh: 核辐射的长期损害导致整个城市及其居民化为粉末。

sentences.en: When I was born, my mom says I looked around the whole hospital room with a stare that said, "This? I've done this before."
sentences.zh: 我出生时，我妈妈说我环顾了整个病房，眼神仿佛在说：“这个？我以前做过这个。”

sentences.en: She says I have old eyes. When my Grandpa Genji died, I was only five years old, but I took my mom by the hand and told her, "Don't worry, he'll come back as a baby."
sentences.zh: 她说我的眼睛老了。当我爷爷源氏去世时，我只有五岁，但我拉着妈妈的手告诉她：“别担心，他会以婴儿的形式回来。”

sentences.en: And yet, for someone who's apparently done this already, I still haven't figured anything out yet.
sentences.zh: 然而，对于显然已经这样做过的人来说，我仍然没有弄清楚任何事情。

sentences.en: My knees still buckle every time I get on a stage.
sentences.zh: 每次我上舞台时，我的膝盖仍然会弯曲。

sentences.en: My self-confidence can be measured out in teaspoons mixed into my poetry, and it still always tastes funny in my mouth.
sentences.zh: 我的自信可以用掺入诗歌的茶匙来衡量，但它在我嘴里的味道仍然很有趣。

sentences.en: But in Hiroshima, some people were wiped clean away, leaving only a wristwatch or a diary page.
sentences.zh: 但在广岛，有些人被清理干净，只留下一块手表或一页日记。

sentences.en: So no matter that I have inhibitions to fill all my pockets, I keep trying, hoping that one day I'll write a poem I can be proud to let sit in a museum exhibit as the only proof I existed.
sentences.zh: 因此，无论我有抑制性地装满我的口袋，我都会继续尝试，希望有一天我能写一首诗，我可以自豪地在博物馆展出，作为我存在的唯一证明。

sentences.en: My parents named me Sarah, which is a biblical name.
sentences.zh: 我父母给我起名叫莎拉，这是一个圣经名字。

sentences.en: In the original story, God told Sarah she could do something impossible, and -- she laughed, because the first Sarah, she didn't know what to do with impossible.
sentences.zh: 在最初的故事中，上帝告诉莎拉她可以做一些不可能的事情，然后——她笑了，因为第一个莎拉，她不知道如何处理不可能的事情。

sentences.en: And me? Well, neither do I, but I see the impossible every day.
sentences.zh: 而我呢？好吧，我也不知道，但我每天都看到不可能的事情。

sentences.en: Impossible is trying to connect in this world, trying to hold onto others while things are blowing up around you, knowing that while you're speaking, they aren't just waiting for their turn to talk -- they hear you.
sentences.zh: 不可能的是在这个世界上尝试与他人建立联系，尝试在周围事情发生时抓住他人，并知道当你说话时，他们不仅仅是在等待轮到他们说话 - 他们会听到你的声音。

sentences.en: They feel exactly what you feel at the same time that you feel it.
sentences.zh: 他们在你感受到的同时也感受到了你的感受。

sentences.en: It's what I strive for every time I open my mouth -- that impossible connection.
sentences.zh: 这就是我每次开口时所努力的目标——那种不可能的联系。

sentences.en: There's this piece of wall in Hiroshima that was completely burnt black by the radiation.
sentences.zh: 广岛有一面墙被辐射完全烧黑了。

sentences.en: But on the front step, a person who was sitting there blocked the rays from hitting the stone.
sentences.zh: 但前面的台阶上，坐着一个人，挡住了光线，没有打在石头上。

sentences.en: The only thing left now is a permanent shadow of positive light.
sentences.zh: 现在唯一剩下的就是正光的永久阴影。

sentences.en: After the A-bomb, specialists said it would take 75 years for the radiation-damaged soil of Hiroshima City to ever grow anything again.
sentences.zh: 原子弹爆炸后，专家表示，广岛市受辐射破坏的土壤需要 75 年才能恢复生长。

sentences.en: But that spring, there were new buds popping up from the earth.
sentences.zh: 但那年春天，地里又长出了新的芽。

sentences.en: When I meet you, in that moment, I'm no longer a part of your future.
sentences.zh: 当我遇见你的那一刻，我就不再是你未来的一部分。

sentences.en: I start quickly becoming part of your past.
sentences.zh: 我开始很快成为你过去的一部分。

sentences.en: But in that instant, I get to share your present.
sentences.zh: 但在那一刻，我可以分享你的礼物。

sentences.en: And you, you get to share mine. And that is the greatest present of all.
sentences.zh: 而你，你可以分享我的。这是最伟大的礼物。

sentences.en: So if you tell me I can do the impossible -- I'll probably laugh at you.
sentences.zh: 所以如果你告诉我我可以完成不可能的事——我可能会嘲笑你。

sentences.en: I don't know if I can change the world yet, because I don't know that much about it -- and I don't know that much about reincarnation either, but if you make me laugh hard enough, sometimes I forget what century I'm in.
sentences.zh: 我还不知道我是否能改变世界，因为我对它了解不多——而且我对轮回也了解不多，但如果你让我笑得够厉害，有时我会忘记自己身处哪个世纪。

sentences.en: This isn't my first time here. This isn't my last time here.
sentences.zh: 这不是我第一次来这里。这不是我最后一次来这里。

sentences.en: These aren't the last words I'll share. But just in case, I'm trying my hardest to get it right this time around.
sentences.zh: 这些不是我要分享的最后一句话。但为了以防万一，我这次会尽最大努力把事情做好。

sentences.en: Thank you. (Applause) Thank you. (Applause) Thank you.
sentences.zh: 谢谢。 （鼓掌）谢谢。 （鼓掌）谢谢。

sentences.en: (Applause) Thank you. (Applause)
sentences.zh: （鼓掌）谢谢。 （掌声）
